as const satisfies T gives readonly literal types plus shape validation.
Brands add a phantom property to simulate nominal types like UserId or Email.
Function-type properties are contravariant in parameters under strictFunctionTypes; method syntax stays bivariant.
Mutable arrays are treated covariantly, which is a known soundness hole.
Prefer @ts-expect-error over @ts-ignore so stale suppressions are reported.

questions.prompt: What is the type of `cfg.port`?
questions.code: const cfg = { port: 3000, host: "localhost" } satisfies Record<string, string | number>;
questions.explanation: satisfies validates against Record<string, string | number> but keeps the inferred type of the expression, so port is number. With an annotation it would be string | number.

questions.prompt: Which line errors?
questions.explanation: satisfies performs excess property checking on the literal, so the typo 'pth' (with path missing) is an error on line A. Line B with an assertion compiles because 'as' only requires the types to be comparable.

questions.prompt: Why does this compile, and what is the problem?
options: Arrays are treated covariantly, so a Cat ends up in a Dog[]
questions.explanation: TypeScript allows Dog[] to be assigned to Animal[] for convenience, even though arrays are mutable. Pushing a cat through the Animal[] alias corrupts the Dog[]. readonly arrays avoid this.

questions.prompt: Under strictFunctionTypes, which assignment errors?
questions.code:
let handleAnimal = (a: Animal) => {};
let handleDog = (d: Dog) => d.bark();
questions.explanation: Function parameters are contravariant. A Dog handler may call bark(), so it is unsafe where any Animal can be passed. An Animal handler is safe where Dogs are passed.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of `@ts-expect-error` over `@ts-ignore`?
options: It reports an error when the next line no longer has an error
It suppresses errors in the whole file
questions.explanation: An unused @ts-expect-error is itself an error, so suppressions are removed once the underlying problem is fixed. @ts-ignore stays silently forever.

questions.prompt: What does this branded type prevent?
questions.code: type UserId = string & { readonly __brand: "UserId" };
options: Passing a plain string or another branded ID where UserId is expected
questions.explanation: The phantom brand property means only values produced by the brand constructor match UserId. At runtime it is just a string, so comparison and serialization work normally.

questions.prompt: Method syntax in an interface (`onEvent(x: Dog): void`) has its parameter checked bivariantly even with strictFunctionTypes on.
questions.explanation: strictFunctionTypes applies only to function type syntax. Methods remain bivariant for compatibility with patterns like Array<T> methods, which is why property syntax is safer for callbacks.

questions.prompt: `x satisfies T` changes the type of `x` to `T`.
questions.explanation: satisfies only checks assignability. The expression keeps its inferred type, which is the whole point compared to an annotation.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which are known places where TypeScript is unsound by design?
questions.explanation: Array covariance, method bivariance, unchecked index reads and assertions all let incorrect programs compile. Discriminated union narrowing is sound.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: `const theme = { primary: "#fff" } as const ___ Record<string, string>` keeps literal readonly types while validating the shape.
questions.explanation: as const satisfies T is the idiom for constants: as const keeps literals and readonly, satisfies validates against the schema type without widening.

questions.prompt: When would you use satisfies instead of a type annotation?
questions.answer: Use satisfies when you want the compiler to validate a value against a type but keep the value's more precise inferred type. Typical cases are config objects, route tables and lookup maps: with const x: Record<string, Route> = {...}, the keys widen to string so x.typo compiles and you lose literal values; with satisfies Record<string, Route> you still get excess property and shape checking, but keyof typeof x is the exact key union and values keep literal types. An annotation is still right when you want the variable to be the wider type, for example a variable that will be reassigned or a public API contract.

questions.prompt: Explain covariance and contravariance with a TypeScript example.
questions.answer: If Dog extends Animal, a type constructor is covariant when Box<Dog> is assignable to Box<Animal>: return types and readonly properties behave this way because you only read Dogs, which are Animals. It is contravariant when the direction flips: a function (a: Animal) => void can be used where (d: Dog) => void is expected, because it can handle any Dog, but not the reverse, since a Dog handler might call bark() on a Cat. Mutable containers should be invariant, but TypeScript treats arrays covariantly for convenience, which is unsound. Under strictFunctionTypes, function-type properties are checked contravariantly while method syntax stays bivariant, so I declare callbacks as properties.

questions.prompt: How do you model nominal types like UserId or Email in a structural type system?
questions.answer: Use branded types: type UserId = string & { readonly __brand: 'UserId' } (or a unique symbol key for stronger privacy). The brand exists only at the type level, so the runtime value is a plain string with no cost. Create values only through a function that validates and then asserts, like parseEmail(s): Email, so the type proves the value was checked (parse, don't validate). Plain strings and other brands are rejected at compile time, preventing ID mix-ups and unvalidated input from reaching functions that require clean data. Zod and Effect Schema support brands directly.
